RT @The_Cyber_News: ‼️ PoC Released for Telegram Desktop Flaw Enabling One-Click File Account Takeover

Details: https://t.co/cxXxKHPrPD

A public proof of concept has exposed a flaw in Telegram Desktop that could let attackers steal local files and take over accounts after a user clicks a crafted external link. 

The weakness lies in how Telegram Desktop handles links opened outside the app. When Telegram is already running, another instance passes the link to it through a local communication channel, known as inter-process communication, or IPC. 

An attacker could place the character inside a crafted link and make Telegram read part of the link as another command. 

#cybersecuritynews

items.content:
RT @zoecyber001: The technical breakdown of how this Telegram Desktop bug (CVE-2026-107181) actually works is wild:
 1. When you click a tg:// link in your browser, the operating system passes it to your open Telegram app over an internal IPC channel.
2. Telegram used semicolons to separate internal IPC commands, but forgot to escape semicolons in web links. An attacker puts a semicolon in a link to break out of the parameter and inject their own internal commands.
3. That injected command tells Telegram to read and send back your local "tdata" folder.
4. The tdata folder holds your raw session tokens. If an attacker copies your tdata folder, they can paste it into their own Telegram and be logged in as you instantly. No SMS, no 2FA prompt, no login alert.
 
Update to 7.2.9 immediately. And turn on a local App Passcode in Telegram settings, which forces the app to encrypt your tdata folder on disk.

items.content:
The user said he had removed the Chrome extension twice.

It still came back.

At first, I thought Chrome Sync was probably restoring it, so we disabled sync and removed the extension again.

After the next restart, it was back.

That was when I stopped looking at Chrome itself and checked the Windows policies controlling the browser.

Inside the Registry, I found this path:

HKLM\SOFTWARE\Policies\Google\Chrome\ExtensionInstallForcelist

There was one extension ID configured there.

That changed the whole investigation.

Chrome was not randomly reinstalling the extension.

Windows policy was telling Chrome that the extension had to be installed.

I checked the extension files under the user’s Chrome profile and found one called:

Secure Search Helper

The name sounded harmless.

But its manifest showed permissions like:

tabs

webRequest

and access to:

<all_urls>

Meaning it potentially had visibility into a lot of what the user was doing inside the browser.

I checked Sysmon next.

Event ID 13 showed that the Chrome policy registry value had been created the previous afternoon.

A few seconds earlier, Sysmon had also recorded reg.exe being launched from PowerShell.

So now we had a proper timeline.

PowerShell runs.

reg.exe modifies Chrome policy.

Chrome sees the forced-extension policy.

The extension installs automatically.

The user removes it.

Chrome checks the policy again and installs it back.

That explained why normal removal was not working.

We isolated the laptop, preserved the Registry entries, extension files and Sysmon logs, then removed the policy after collecting the evidence.

We also revoked the user’s active sessions because with a browser extension like this, I would not be comfortable assuming only browsing history was exposed.

The part I found interesting was that the user actually did the right thing.

He saw an extension he did not recognise and removed it.

The problem was sitting one level deeper.

As long as that Registry policy remained there, Chrome was simply going to bring the extension back.

So if you ever remove a suspicious Chrome extension and it keeps reinstalling itself, don't only check the browser.

Check the policies controlling the browser too.

Sometimes Chrome is not the one making the decision.

items.content:
one of the annoying parts of building an ai based vulnerability scanner is that there is no free lunch. you get completely different results depending on how you approach the problem.

1. you can throw an absurd number of tokens at gpt sol, and it will still miss a bug that opus finds, same applies other way around

2. different prompts and initial conditions send agents down completely different paths, exploring different ideas and finding different bugs.

3. some vulnerabilities only come up when you build task specific environments and feedback loops that let agents explore and hill climb. no amount of generic prompting would uncover them, these are the vulnerabilities where human operator matters a lot

the list goes on and you will find some weird edge case that leads to vulnerability every time you approach in different way.
